splits.text: The model avoids work that will later be discarded.
The model performs necessary work only once even when an expression is used multiple times.

expansions.text: Optimal parallel reduction treats duplication and erasure as scheduling costs rather than unavoidable consequences of syntax.

splits.text: Confluence asks whether different valid reduction choices can produce different results.
The one-step diamond property requires either one-step result to reach a common net after one further interaction.

expansions.text: A reduction choice is a valid local interaction available in the current net.

splits.text: Each active pair owns the only principal port of each participating agent.
Distinct active pairs therefore use distinct agents.
Rewrites of distinct active pairs commute and preserve the same nearby wiring.

expansions.text: Disjoint principal ports prevent two simultaneous rewrites from modifying the same agent.

splits.text: The diamond property concerns agreement between competing local steps.
The diamond property does not imply that reduction terminates.
For a normalizing core interaction order, every normalizing order reaches the same result in the same number of interactions.

expansions.text: Termination means that no infinite sequence of reductions exists.

splits.text: Earlier approaches represented each sharing scope with indexed fans and delimiter agents.
Delimiter agents included brackets, croissants, and related constructs.
Delimiter interactions could outnumber the useful fan work.
Some earlier systems allowed indices to grow without bound.

expansions.text: The variable-arity replicator is intended to encode sharing without maintaining a separate delimiter structure for every scope.

splits.text: Application and function fans are triangles with a top principal port and two fixed bottom auxiliary positions.
Replicators are trapezoids with a centered top principal port and evenly spaced bottom auxiliary ports.
Rectangles denote fragments or wire endpoints rather than agents.
An eraser has only a principal port.

expansions.text: The shapes encode port conventions so diagrams can distinguish agent structure from labels and endpoints.

splits.text: A replicator may have any natural-number arity.
A replicator joins the uses of one shared value.
The replicator stores a sharing context as a level on the agent and a delta on each auxiliary port.

expansions.text: Arity is the number of auxiliary ports on a replicator.

splits.text: Linear terms use each bound variable exactly once.
Affine terms use each bound variable at most once.
Relevant terms use each bound variable at least once.
Full terms permit any number of uses.
Fans encode structure, erasers encode omission, and replicators encode sharing.
Equal replicators must match in level, arity, and every port delta.
Well-formed λ-term translations make same-level active replicators equal.
Hand-built nets cannot compare replicator levels alone.

expansions.text: Level-only comparison is sound only when the construction invariant already guarantees matching arity and deltas.

splits.text: Parent and child are orientation labels on a wire relative to the root.
Canonical nets begin with unpaired fan-in replicators whose auxiliaries are parents and principal is a child.
Reduction can create fan-outs with the opposite orientation.
A fan-out is paired upstream with at least one fan-in, but a fan-in need not have a partner.
Levels and deltas provide local evidence for pairing.

expansions.text: The root is the distinguished top entry from which parent–child orientation is read.

splits.text: Equal agents annihilate each other.
In a well-formed λ translation, same-level active replicators annihilate and matching auxiliary ports reconnect.
Fan annihilation represents applying a λ abstraction to its argument.

expansions.text: Annihilation removes the active pair and preserves connectivity by joining corresponding auxiliary wires.

splits.text: An eraser passes through one auxiliary port of a distinct agent at a time.
A two-port fan meeting an eraser leaves two erasers connected to its auxiliary outputs.
An n-port replicator meeting an eraser leaves n erasers.

expansions.text: Erasure propagates by replacing the erased agent with one eraser per outgoing auxiliary connection.

splits.text: Applications and abstractions use the same triangular fan shape.
Their roles are identified by wire orientation relative to the root.
Principal-to-principal fan interaction removes both fans and reconnects matching auxiliary ports.
Auxiliary ports are ordered clockwise when the principal port points down.
The fan interaction represents β-reduction.

expansions.text: Rotation changes how an auxiliary port appears geometrically without changing its semantic index.

splits.text: The downward application fan orders its auxiliaries left-to-right as first and second.
The rotated upward abstraction fan orders its auxiliaries right-to-left as first and second.
Matching semantic port indices can therefore cross the drawn wires.

expansions.text: Wire crossing in this diagram records index-preserving reconnection, not an additional crossing agent.

splits.text: A replicator meeting a fan produces one exact fan copy per replicator auxiliary port.
The fan produces one fan per auxiliary port of the replicator.
Each resulting agent retains its original role in the other agent’s surrounding context.
Matching levels allow annihilation in a well-formed λ translation.
Annihilation removes both replicators and reconnects matching auxiliary ports.
Annihilation creates no replicas.
Hand-built nets require matching arity and every port delta in addition to matching levels.
When levels differ, the replicators commute rather than annihilate.
The lower-level replicator creates one higher-level replica per auxiliary port.
The higher-level replicator creates exact lower-level replicas per auxiliary port.
Each higher-level replica adds the exit-port delta to its current level.
Duplicate means an exact copy.
Replicate allows copies whose levels differ.
Deltas may be negative, zero, or positive.

expansions.text: Level adjustment lets one replication rule carry context information that indexed delimiters represented explicitly in older systems.

splits.text: Each calculus has a bijection from terms to canonical Δ-Nets.
Every term maps to one canonical net.
Each canonical net maps back to one term.
Translation builds a larger net inductively from translated subterms.

expansions.text: A bijection is reversible and one-to-one, so neither terms nor canonical nets are duplicated by the translation.

splits.text: Each fragment has one incoming wire and zero or more outgoing wires.
The outermost fragment connects to a single root.
Free variables become named interface nodes.
The fragment interface allows a translated subterm to plug into its parent.
A free variable remains a named node at the canonical net interface.
A bound occurrence has no variable agent.
A single bound use connects directly to its owning abstraction.
Several bound uses connect through a replicator.
A replicator connects the abstraction’s variable port to multiple concrete use sites.
For λx.x x, the two replicator auxiliaries connect to the application’s argument and function ports.
A one-port zero-delta replicator is omitted because it is equivalent to a wire.

expansions.text: The replicator turns one incoming bound value into independently connected consumer paths.

splits.text: The abstraction’s second auxiliary port represents its bound parameter.
An unused parameter port terminates at an eraser in ΔA and ΔK.
A single use connects directly to the parameter port.
Multiple uses connect through a replicator.
The abstraction’s first auxiliary port represents its body.
In λx.x x, the body port connects to the application result and the replicator ports connect to the function and argument.
The application result uses the first auxiliary port.
The argument fragment uses the second auxiliary port.
The function fragment meets the principal port.
This wiring lets an abstraction on the function side form a β-redex.
The whole term starts at level 0.
Abstraction bodies inherit their abstraction’s level.
An application keeps the function at the current level.
An application assigns the argument level one greater than the current level.
These levels track sharing contexts rather than runtime closure contents.
The outer application gives the function occurrence level 0.
The outer application gives its argument subtree level 1.
The inner application keeps g at level 1 and gives its argument x level 2.
The binder’s replicator is at level 1.
The resulting deltas are ⟨−1, +1⟩.
Each bound occurrence connects to one auxiliary port of its replicator.
The port delta equals the occurrence level minus the replicator level.

expansions.text: Subtracting the replicator level stores only the relative context needed when the port is later traversed.

splits.text: A level delta is not a copy count.
A level delta is not a source-level variable value.
A two-port replicator already records two consumers of one bound value.
Levels and deltas record relative sharing contexts at consumer sites.
Commuting replicators use deltas to adjust replica levels.

expansions.text: The bookkeeping encodes scope-sensitive sharing without explicit scope-delimiter agents.

splits.text: Erasure canonicalization is a global cleanup pass rather than a principal-port interaction.
The sweep starts at the distinguished root and marks reachable material.
Unmarked graph material is deleted.
Deleting an unmarked node can expose a surviving connection that must be terminated by an eraser.
For consecutive replicators A and B, the condition is 0 ≤ lB − lA ≤ d.
The condition proves that B is unpaired when A is known unpaired.
The proof says B cannot interact before A is annihilated.
The inequality is a safety proof rather than a performance heuristic.

expansions.text: Because the required predecessor annihilation never occurs for an unpaired A, the guarded successor is also safely unpaired.

splits.text: ΔK removes auxiliary ports of unpaired replicators that lead directly to erasers.
A remaining one-port zero-delta replicator collapses to a wire.

expansions.text: Decay removes consumers known to produce no surviving output before simplifying the resulting connection.

splits.text: Core interaction rules are locally confluent.
Canonicalization can modify ports outside principal-to-principal pairs.
A schedule is therefore required for canonicalization.
Leftmost-outermost chooses an outermost reducible pattern and then the leftmost candidate.
The schedule is used for ΔA, ΔI, and ΔK so cleanup runs early and merges precede later commutations.
The bijection φ creates the initial canonical net.
Core interactions may move the net into the broader space of proper nets.
The subsystem’s interaction order and canonicalizations are collected by Ω.
The net is read back by φ−1 only after it is normal and canonical.

expansions.text: Separating φ, Ω, and φ−1 prevents intermediate proper nets from being mistaken for final canonical encodings.

splits.text: ΔL has fan annihilation as its only interaction.
Every proper ΔL net is already canonical.
If a λL term normalizes in n β-reductions, its ΔL encoding normalizes in n interactions regardless of order.
ΔA, ΔI, and ΔK add canonicalization for erasure and sharing structure.
The nonlinear systems require canonicalization and a global schedule for the whole-algorithm claim.
The paper claims Church–Rosser confluence and optimality for those systems.
Church–Rosser means divergent paths can be continued to a common result.
Church–Rosser does not require the paths to agree after one step.
Δ-Nets encode each sharing context in a variable-arity replicator.
Reduction combines local interactions with limited global scheduling discipline.
The discipline is intended to prevent avoidable work.

expansions.text: The design moves complexity from explicit scope delimiters into local level-and-delta metadata plus selective scheduling.
